input:
When it comes to running a centrifugal pump, one of the most crucial concepts to grasp is how the pump's performance responds when its rotational speed is changed. The affinity laws provide a powerful and elegant framework for describing exactly this behaviour, and they are widely regarded as essential knowledge for anyone who works with pumping systems on a day-to-day basis.

At their core, the affinity laws describe three simple proportionalities that link performance to speed. The volumetric flow rate is directly proportional to the speed, which means that when the speed goes up, the flow rises in step with it. The head, meanwhile, is proportional to the square of the speed, reflecting the way the energy imparted to the liquid builds as the impeller turns faster. The power, in turn, is proportional to the cube of the speed, underscoring just how steeply the energy demand can climb with even modest speed increases.

A worked check helps to bring the point home. If the speed of the pump is doubled, the power requirement does not simply double alongside the flow; instead, it increases by a factor of 8, climbing to 8 times its original value. It is important to note that all three quantities shift together, so a speed adjustment is never only about flow. The whole operating point moves at once, with significant implications for motor sizing, energy consumption, and the wider system as a whole.
target:
Doubling the speed of a centrifugal pump multiplies the power it draws by 8. The affinity laws state the full set of proportions behind that result, and the power proportion is the one to check before any speed increase is made on an installed pump.

The affinity laws describe one pump at varying rotational speed, with the impeller unchanged and the same liquid handled throughout. Flow varies in direct proportion to speed, so a pump at twice the speed delivers twice the flow. Head varies with the square of the speed. Power varies with the cube of the speed, and rises fastest of the three quantities as speed increases.

The proportions compare duties of a single machine, and they do not rate a different pump. A speed change also fixes all three quantities at once: a change chosen to gain flow raises the head and the power in their stated proportions at the same time.

The worked check tests the power proportion alone. Doubling the speed makes the speed ratio two, and the power ratio is the cube of the speed ratio. Cubing two returns the factor of 8 stated at the start, and the check closes there: the power at the doubled speed stands at eight times the power at the original speed, and the motor and drive sized for the original duty must carry the increase.
